learn.title: 1 — Congress: Structure, The 5 B's, Qualifications & Powers (Article I)
learn.body:
Article I establishes a bicameral national legislature composed of the House of Representatives and the Senate. To easily master Congress, remember 'The 5 B's of Congress':

  • Bicameral — Two distinct chambers balancing population-based representation (House) and state equality (Senate).
  • Bills — Drafting, amending, and passing federal legislation through specialized committees.
  • Budget — Exercising the Power of the Purse; note the Origination Clause (Art. I, Sec. 7): all revenue/tax bills must originate in the House.
  • Balancing Powers & Oversight — Investigating executive agencies, conducting hearings, and holding the power of Impeachment (House impeaches by simple majority; Senate tries and convicts by 2/3 majority).
  • Boundaries & Bipartisanship — Managing district apportionments, coalition building, and Senate advice & consent.

Constitutional Qualifications Mnemonic (Increasing Rule: 25/7/2 vs 30/9/6):

  • House: Minimum age 25, citizen for 7 years, elected every 2 years (inhabitant of state).
  • Senate: Minimum age 30, citizen for 9 years, elected every 6 years (inhabitant of state).

Article I, Section 8 Powers: Tax, borrow money, coin money, regulate commerce, establish lower federal courts, declare war, raise military forces (Air Force added by statute), and the Elastic Clause (Necessary and Proper Clause) which stretches federal powers to execute enumerated responsibilities.

learn.title: 2 — Leadership, Committees, Gerrymandering & Apportionment
learn.body:
Congressional Leadership:

  • House: Speaker of the House (Rep. Mike Johnson) is the most powerful officer, elected by the entire body, partisan leader of the majority, and second in line to the presidency (behind the VP). The Constitution does NOT require the Speaker to be an elected House member. House Minority Leader is Rep. Hakeem Jeffries. Whips 'whip up' votes and enforce party discipline.
  • Senate: No Speaker. Constitutional President of the Senate is the Vice President (JD Vance), who only breaks ties. The real legislative leader is the Senate Majority Leader (Sen. John Thune), alongside the Minority Leader (Sen. Chuck Schumer).

Congressional Committees:

  • Standing Committees — Permanent panels (first stop for proposed bills).
  • Most Important House Committee — The House Rules Committee (the 'Traffic Cop' of the House, deciding which bills reach the floor, setting time limits, and restricting amendments) alongside the House Ways and Means Committee (taxation/revenue).
  • Conference Committees — Temporary ad hoc panels reconciling differing House and Senate versions of a bill.
  • Select / Ad Hoc Committees — Temporary panels formed for specific investigations (e.g., House Oversight).

Apportionment & Gerrymandering: House seats are capped at 435 (Reapportionment Act of 1929). Every 10 years, seats are reapportioned among states using the equal proportions method based on Decennial Census data. Gerrymandering is the manipulative redrawing of legislative district boundaries for partisan advantage. The most famous mid-decade partisan redistricting occurred in 2003 (Texas).

learn.title: 3 — Budget, $40T Debt, Filibuster, Cloture & Nuclear Option
learn.body:
Federal Budget & National Debt:

  • The federal fiscal year runs from October 1 to September 30. Congress must pass 12 separate appropriation bills by September 30. If delayed, Congress passes a Continuing Resolution (CR) to keep agencies open.
  • The U.S. National Debt is approximately $40 Trillion. The main causes highlighted in class are: (1) mandatory entitlement spending (Social Security and Medicare/Medicaid), (2) net interest on the national debt, (3) defense spending, and (4) structural revenue shortfalls from major tax cuts.

Senate Procedures: Filibuster, Cloture & Nuclear Option:

  • The filibuster allows extended floor debate to delay or block bills. Ending debate requires Cloture (Senate Rule 22), requiring a three-fifths majority (60 votes).
  • The Nuclear Option — Changing Senate operating procedures with a simple majority (51 votes):
  • 2013 (Democrats / Harry Reid): Lowered confirmation threshold to simple majority for executive nominees and lower federal court judges.
  • 2017 (Republicans / Mitch McConnell): Extended the nuclear option to Supreme Court nominations (to confirm Neil Gorsuch).
  • 2019 (Republicans): Reduced post-cloture floor debate time for lower nominees.
  • Budget Reconciliation — 1974 statutory process allowing tax, spending, and debt-limit bills to pass the Senate with a simple majority (51 votes), completely exempt from filibusters.

learn.title: 4 — The Presidency: Design, Powers & Executive Orders (Article II)
learn.body:
Article II vests executive power in a single President elected by the Electoral College (538 total votes, 270 to win; 48 states winner-take-all, Nebraska & Maine award by congressional district). Qualifications: at least 35 years old, natural born citizen, and 14 years a U.S. resident. Serves a 4-year term, limited to 2 terms (22nd Amendment).

Core Powers of the President:

  • Veto Power — Veto bills passed by Congress; overridden only by a 2/3 vote in both chambers.
  • Commander-in-Chief — Commands armed forces; only Congress can declare war.
  • Appointment Power — Appoints ambassadors, SCOTUS justices, federal judges, and 'other officers' with Senate confirmation.
  • Treaty Power — Negotiates treaties with 2/3 Senate approval.
  • Pardon Power — Unchecked power for federal crimes and treason, but CANNOT pardon in cases of impeachment.
  • Take Care Clause — Duty to ensure laws are faithfully executed.

Executive Orders & Presidential Theories:

  • Franklin D. Roosevelt (FDR) issued the most executive orders in U.S. history (3,728 EOs), using them aggressively to implement the New Deal and manage the Great Depression.
  • Theodore Roosevelt championed the 'Stewardship Theory' of executive power, famously declaring: 'My critics may call me a dictator, but I am proud to say that I have used every ounce of power the Constitution gave me... I did not usurp power, but I did greatly broaden the use of executive power.'
  • Executive orders carry the force of law without congressional votes; popular examples include the Emancipation Proclamation and military desegregation, while controversial orders include Japanese-American internment (EO 9066), travel bans, and student loan cancellations.

learn.title: 5 — Testing Executive Authority: War Powers, Emergencies & Statutory Limits
learn.body:
War Powers & Recent Conflicts:

  • The War Powers Resolution of 1973 requires the President to notify Congress within 48 hours of introducing troops into hostilities and withdraw them within 60 days unless Congress authorizes force.
  • The two recent conflicts that tested the constitutionality of the Commander-in-Chief powers versus Congress's power to declare war are Venezuela and Iran.
  • NATO Withdrawal Authority: Can the President unilaterally withdraw the U.S. from NATO? NO — federal statute (NDAA) explicitly prohibits any president from withdrawing from NATO without a 2/3 Senate vote or an Act of Congress.

Statutory Limits & Emergency Powers:

  • Impoundment Control Act of 1974 — Enforces the 'Power of the Purse' (Article I, Sec. 9). The President cannot refuse to spend money appropriated by Congress without congressional approval. A 'Pocket Rescission' occurs when a cancellation request is submitted too late for Congress to act before funds expire (e.g., USAID).
  • Alien Enemies Act of 1798 — Wartime law permitting detention and deportation of hostile foreign nationals without normal judicial due process.
  • Domestic Military Deployment: The Posse Comitatus Act of 1878 strictly forbids using federal military forces for civilian domestic policing. The Insurrection Act of 1807 is the primary exception, allowing the President to deploy troops domestically to suppress rebellions or enforce federal laws when state authorities fail.
  • Tariffs: Congress delegated tariff adjustments under the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 based on national security findings.

learn.title: 6 — The Judiciary: Structure, Article III & Marbury v. Madison (1789 & 1803)
learn.body:
Article III vests judicial power in one Supreme Court and inferior courts established by Congress. Federal judges hold office 'during good Behaviour' (lifetime tenure unless impeached), nominated by the President and confirmed by Senate majority vote. The Constitution sets no age, citizenship, or legal degree requirements.

The Judiciary Act of 1789 (Memorize this date!):

  • Created the three-tier federal court system: District Courts (federal trial courts) and Circuit Courts (courts of appeals).
  • Article III, Section 2 limits Original Jurisdiction (SCOTUS hears first) to cases involving ambassadors, public ministers, consuls, and disputes between states. All other cases fall under Appellate Jurisdiction.

Marbury v. Madison (1803) & Judicial Review:

  • William Marbury petitioned for a Writ of Mandamus (order compelling an official to perform a duty) because James Madison withheld his judicial commission. Marbury cited Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789.
  • Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that Section 13 unconstitutionally expanded the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction beyond Article III.
  • This established Judicial Review — the power of the judiciary to strike down laws conflicting with the Constitution: 'A law repugnant to the constitution is void.'

learn.title: 7 — Judicial Philosophies, Precedent & Landmark Cases
learn.body:
Judicial Philosophies & Doctrines:

  • Originalism / Textualism — Interprets the Constitution according to the text and original public understanding at ratification.
  • Living Constitution / Evolutionism — Interprets constitutional principles dynamically to adapt to evolving modern societal standards.
  • Stare Decisis — Latin for 'to stand by things decided'; the principle that courts must follow established judicial precedents.
  • Emergency Docket ('Shadow Docket') — Expedited emergency rulings and injunctions issued by the Supreme Court without full merits briefing, oral argument, or detailed opinions.

Recent Key Landmark Decisions:

  • Dobbs v. Jackson (2022) — Overturned Roe v. Wade; ruled the Constitution does not guarantee a right to abortion, returning regulation to states.
  • West Virginia v. EPA (2022) — Established the Major Questions Doctrine; administrative agencies cannot issue major regulations of vast economic/political significance without clear statutory authorization from Congress.
  • Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022) — Upheld high school football coach's right to pray at midfield under Free Exercise and Free Speech.
  • Trump v. United States (2024) — Held presidents have absolute immunity for core constitutional executive duties, presumptive immunity for official acts, and no immunity for unofficial acts.

learn.title: 8 — Political Parties, Realignment, Georgia Transition & Elections
learn.body:
Polarization & Modern Parties (Specific Test Topic):

Political parties work to win elections and implement policy by drafting legislation, guiding party votes, nominating candidates, and mobilizing voters. Modern partisan polarization has intensified divisive wedge issues, normalized aggressive/rude rhetoric during hearings (e.g., MTG, AOC, and Jasmine Crockett trading insults at House Oversight hearings), and magnified the influence of elite billionaire megadonors.

Party Realignment & Third Parties:

  • Party Realignment — Major shifts in voter coalitions. Modern Republican realignment includes shifts among blue-collar union workers, men of color (Hispanic men 45% → 54%, Black men 12% → 20%), and young men (35% → 42%).
  • Bull Moose Party (1912 / Teddy Roosevelt) — Women's suffrage, social insurance, 8-hour workday, campaign reform.
  • Reform Party (1992 / Ross Perot) — Eliminating national debt, campaign finance reform, term limits (won 19% popular vote).

Georgia Political Transition:

Georgia was solidly Democratic from 1872 to 2002. In 2001, Democratic Governor Roy Barnes led the controversial initiative to change the Georgia state flag to remove the 1956 Confederate emblem. Severe voter backlash fractured rural Democratic support, electing Sonny Perdue in 2002 (took office 2003) as Georgia's first Republican governor since Reconstruction and transforming Georgia into a Republican state.

Election Types:

  • Primaries: Closed (party members only), Open (voter picks either ballot), Blanket / Jungle (all candidates on one ballot).
  • General Elections: Plurality (most votes wins), Majority (>50% required; triggers Runoff if missed, like GA), and Ranked Choice Voting (instant runoff redistribution).

paragraphs.text: The 5 B's of Congress encapsulate its structure and responsibilities: Bicameral organization, passing Bills, managing the federal Budget (Power of the Purse), Balancing power through executive oversight and impeachment, and managing electoral Boundaries and Bipartisanship. All revenue bills must originate in the House of Representatives under the Origination Clause (Article I, Section 7). Qualifications: House members must be at least 25 years old and citizens for 7 years (2-year terms); Senators must be at least 30 years old and citizens for 9 years (6-year terms). The Elastic Clause (Article I, Section 8, Clause 18) empowers Congress to make all laws necessary and proper for executing its powers.

In the House, the Speaker of the House (Mike Johnson) is the most powerful officer, elected by the full chamber and second in line to the presidency. The Constitution does not require the Speaker to be an elected member of Congress. The most powerful committee in the House is the House Rules Committee, known as the 'Traffic Cop' because it sets the terms of floor debate and amendment rules, alongside Ways and Means. In the Senate, the Vice President (JD Vance) serves as President of the Senate, while Majority Leader John Thune and Minority Leader Chuck Schumer direct floor activity. Apportionment uses the equal proportions method based on census data every ten years for the 435 House seats. Gerrymandering remains a contentious tactic, with Texas undergoing a prominent mid-decade redistricting in 2003.

The federal fiscal year runs from October 1 to September 30, requiring 12 appropriation bills. When delayed, Congress enacts Continuing Resolutions. The U.S. National Debt is approximately $40 trillion, driven by mandatory entitlement spending on Social Security and Medicare, interest on the national debt, defense, and tax revenue gaps. Senate filibusters require 60 votes (three-fifths majority) under Cloture Rule 22 to end debate. The Nuclear Option was used by Democrats in 2013 for lower judges and executive nominees, and extended by Republicans in 2017 to Supreme Court nominees (Neil Gorsuch). Budget Reconciliation bypasses the filibuster with a simple 51-vote majority.

Article II vests executive power in a President elected by the Electoral College (538 total, 270 to win; Maine and Nebraska award by district). Qualifications require being at least 35 years old, a natural-born citizen, and 14 years a resident. The President holds veto, appointment, treaty (2/3 Senate), and pardon powers (cannot pardon impeachment). Franklin D. Roosevelt issued the most executive orders in history (3,728) to combat the Great Depression. Theodore Roosevelt championed broad executive authority, stating critics might call him a dictator but he used every ounce of constitutional power to broaden executive authority.

The War Powers Resolution of 1973 mandates 48-hour notification and a 60-day troop withdrawal limit without congressional authorization; recent conflicts testing these powers include Venezuela and Iran. The President lacks the authority to withdraw unilaterally from NATO, as federal law requires a two-thirds Senate vote or an Act of Congress. The Impoundment Control Act of 1974 bars presidents from withholding appropriated funds. The Posse Comitatus Act of 1878 forbids civilian domestic military policing, while the Insurrection Act of 1807 serves as the primary statutory exception allowing domestic deployment during rebellions.

The Judiciary Act of 1789 created the three-tier federal court system: District Courts and Circuit Courts under the Supreme Court. Article III grants lifetime tenure during good behavior with no explicit age or degree requirements. In Marbury v. Madison (1803), Chief Justice John Marshall established Judicial Review, holding that Section 13 of the 1789 Act unconstitutionally expanded the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction, declaring that any law repugnant to the Constitution is void.

Judicial interpretation splits between Originalism (original public meaning at ratification) and Living Constitution / Evolutionism (evolving modern values). Stare Decisis dictates adhering to precedent. Key cases include Dobbs v. Jackson (2022, overturning Roe v. Wade), West Virginia v. EPA (2022, Major Questions Doctrine), Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022, prayer rights), and Trump v. United States (2024, presidential immunity for official acts). The Court also uses the Emergency Shadow Docket for rapid unsigned orders.

Political parties organize to win elections and steer policy. Partisan polarization has heightened divisive issues, normalized uncivil behavior in hearings (such as insults between MTG, AOC, and Jasmine Crockett in House Oversight), and elevated billionaire donor influence. Realignment examples include the Republican MAGA shift with blue-collar workers and men of color. Key third parties include Roosevelt's Bull Moose Party (1912) and Ross Perot's Reform Party (1992). In Georgia, Governor Roy Barnes changed the state flag in 2001, triggering backlash that elected Sonny Perdue in 2002/2003 as the first Republican governor since Reconstruction. Election systems feature open, closed, and blanket primaries, alongside plurality, majority (runoffs), and ranked choice voting.

anki.q: What are 'The 5 B's of Congress'?
anki.a: 1. Bicameral (House & Senate) | 2. Bills (passing legislation) | 3. Budget (Power of the Purse) | 4. Balancing power (oversight & impeachment) | 5. Boundaries & Bipartisanship.

anki.q: What does the Origination Clause (Article I, Section 7) dictate regarding budget bills?
anki.a: All bills for raising revenue (taxes and budgets) MUST originate in the House of Representatives.

anki.q: What are the age and citizenship requirements for the House vs. Senate? (Mnemonic: 25/7/2 vs 30/9/6)
anki.a: House: 25 years old, 7 years citizen, 2-year term. | Senate: 30 years old, 9 years citizen, 6-year term.

anki.q: What is the Elastic Clause and where is it in the Constitution?
anki.a: Article I, Section 8, Clause 18 (Necessary and Proper Clause) — gives Congress implied powers to pass all laws necessary and proper to carry out its enumerated powers.

anki.q: What is the size of the U.S. National Debt today and what are its four main causes?
anki.a: Approximately $40 Trillion. Caused by: (1) Mandatory entitlement spending (Social Security & Medicare), (2) Net interest on national debt, (3) Defense spending, (4) Structural revenue deficits from tax cuts.

anki.q: What two recent international conflicts tested the President's Commander-in-Chief powers vs Congress's power to declare war?
anki.a: Venezuela and Iran.

anki.q: Does the Executive Branch have the authority to unilaterally withdraw the U.S. from NATO?
anki.a: NO. Federal law (NDAA statute) requires either a 2/3 supermajority vote in the Senate or an authorizing Act of Congress to withdraw from NATO.

anki.q: What year was the Judiciary Act passed and what federal courts did it create?
anki.a: 1789. It created the District Courts (federal trial courts) and Circuit Courts (courts of appeals) under the Supreme Court.

anki.q: Who are the current congressional leaders in the House and Senate?
anki.a: House Speaker: Mike Johnson (R) | House Minority Leader: Hakeem Jeffries (D) | Senate Majority Leader: John Thune (R) | Senate Minority Leader: Chuck Schumer (D) | Senate President: JD Vance (VP).

anki.q: Which committee is considered the most powerful in the House of Representatives?
anki.a: The House Rules Committee ('Traffic Cop' of the House — controls which bills reach the floor, debate time, and amendment rules), alongside Ways and Means (taxes).

anki.q: What is gerrymandering and how many voting seats are in the House?
anki.a: Gerrymandering is manipulating district boundaries to favor one party. The House is capped at 435 voting members by the Reapportionment Act of 1929.

anki.q: What is the Cloture threshold in the Senate to end a filibuster on legislation?
anki.a: Three-fifths of all sworn senators (60 votes) under Senate Rule 22.

anki.q: Explain the Nuclear Option in 2013 vs 2017.
anki.a: 2013 (Democrats/Harry Reid): lowered nominee confirmation threshold to simple majority (51 votes) for executive and lower court judges. 2017 (Republicans/Mitch McConnell): extended simple majority to Supreme Court nominations (Neil Gorsuch).

anki.q: Which U.S. President issued the most executive orders in history and why?
anki.a: Franklin D. Roosevelt (FDR) with 3,728 executive orders, using them extensively to create New Deal agencies, fight the Great Depression, and manage WWII mobilization.

anki.q: What was Theodore Roosevelt's famous quote/philosophy on executive power?
anki.a: Stewardship Theory: 'My critics may call me a dictator, but I am proud to say that I have used every ounce of power the Constitution gave me... I did not usurp power, but I did greatly broaden the use of executive power.'

anki.q: What does the Impoundment Control Act of 1974 prevent the President from doing?
anki.a: It forbids the President from refusing to spend funds appropriated by Congress (defending Article I's 'Power of the Purse').

anki.q: What are the rules and time limits of the War Powers Resolution of 1973?
anki.a: Notify Congress within 48 hours of deploying troops into hostilities; withdraw troops within 60 days unless Congress authorizes force or declares war.

anki.q: Distinguish between the Posse Comitatus Act (1878) and the Insurrection Act (1807).
anki.a: Posse Comitatus (1878) strictly prohibits using federal military for civilian domestic law enforcement. Insurrection Act (1807) is the major exception allowing military deployment to suppress insurrections or enforce federal law.

anki.q: What was the ruling and constitutional reasoning in Marbury v. Madison (1803)?
anki.a: Established Judicial Review. Chief Justice John Marshall ruled Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional because Congress cannot expand SCOTUS original jurisdiction beyond Article III. 'A law repugnant to the constitution is void.'

anki.q: What is Stare Decisis?
anki.a: Latin for 'to stand by things decided'; the judicial doctrine requiring judges to follow established legal precedents in future cases.

anki.q: What factors characterize modern partisan polarization discussed in class?
anki.a: Deepening divisive wedge issues, normalized rude/toxic rhetoric (e.g., MTG, AOC & Jasmine Crockett trading insults at House Oversight hearings), and the heavy influence of elite billionaire donors.

anki.q: What catalytic event triggered Georgia's party realignment in 2001–2003?
anki.a: In 2001, Democratic Gov. Roy Barnes removed the 1956 Confederate emblem from the state flag. Conservative rural backlash led to Sonny Perdue (2002/2003) becoming the first Republican governor since Reconstruction.

anki.q: What were the key issues of the Bull Moose Party (1912) and Reform Party (1992)?
anki.a: Bull Moose (Teddy Roosevelt): Women's suffrage, social insurance, 8-hour workday. Reform Party (Ross Perot): Reducing national debt, term limits, campaign finance reform.

anki.q: What are the three primary election types?
anki.a: Closed (registered party members only), Open (any voter selects either primary ballot), and Blanket/Jungle (all candidates from all parties on a single ballot).

anki.q: What is the difference between Plurality and Majority voting systems?
anki.a: Plurality: candidate with the most votes wins. Majority: candidate must win >50% (triggers a runoff between top two finishers if not met, like in Georgia).

anki.q: What is the Supreme Court's Emergency 'Shadow' Docket?
anki.a: Emergency orders and stays issued rapidly by SCOTUS without full briefing, oral argument, or lengthy explanatory opinions.

anki.q: What was the core holding in Dobbs v. Jackson (2022)?
anki.a: Overturned Roe v. Wade; held that the U.S. Constitution does not confer a right to abortion, returning regulation to the states.

anki.q: What is the Major Questions Doctrine from West Virginia v. EPA (2022)?
anki.a: Regulatory agencies cannot decide issues of vast economic and political significance without clear, explicit authorization from Congress.

anki.q: What immunity was established in Trump v. United States (2024)?
anki.a: Presidents have absolute immunity for core constitutional acts, presumptive immunity for official acts, and no immunity for unofficial private acts.

anki.q: What are the start and end dates of the federal fiscal year?
anki.a: October 1 to September 30.

quiz.q: Under Article I, Section 7 of the U.S. Constitution (the Origination Clause), where MUST all revenue and tax bills originate?
options: In the Department of the Treasury
In the Executive Office of the President
quiz.explanation: The Origination Clause explicitly states that all bills for raising revenue shall originate in the House of Representatives.

quiz.q: Which committee is considered the most powerful 'Traffic Cop' of the House of Representatives, setting the terms for floor debate and amendments?
quiz.explanation: The House Rules Committee is the powerful 'Traffic Cop' that decides whether and when bills reach the House floor, sets debate time limits, and determines allowable amendments.

quiz.q: What are the two recent international conflicts cited in lecture that tested the President's Commander-in-Chief powers against Congress's power to declare war?
quiz.explanation: Venezuela and Iran were specifically highlighted as modern flashpoints testing unilateral presidential war powers versus congressional war declarations under the War Powers Resolution.

quiz.q: Does the President of the United States possess the unilateral authority to withdraw from NATO?
options: Yes, the Executive Vesting Clause gives plenary foreign policy withdrawal power
Yes, via a unilateral Executive Order
No, federal statute explicitly requires a 2/3 Senate vote or an Act of Congress
No, withdrawal requires approval from the Supreme Court
quiz.explanation: Congress enacted explicit statutory language (NDAA) prohibiting any President from withdrawing from NATO without a 2/3 Senate supermajority or an authorizing Act of Congress.

quiz.q: Which U.S. President issued the greatest number of executive orders in American history (over 3,700 EOs)?
quiz.explanation: FDR issued 3,728 executive orders—by far the most in history—using them to create New Deal emergency agencies to fight the Great Depression and direct WWII mobilization.

quiz.q: What year was the landmark Judiciary Act passed that established the federal District and Circuit court system?
quiz.explanation: The Judiciary Act of 1789 created the three-tier federal judicial hierarchy (District Courts, Circuit Courts of Appeals, Supreme Court).

quiz.q: What vote is required in the Senate to invoke Cloture under Rule 22 to break a filibuster on legislation?
quiz.explanation: Under Senate Rule 22, invoking Cloture to end debate on legislation requires 60 votes (three-fifths of the Senate).

quiz.q: What is the primary difference between the Posse Comitatus Act of 1878 and the Insurrection Act of 1807?
options: Posse Comitatus bans domestic military law enforcement; Insurrection Act provides the statutory exception for suppressing insurrections
Posse Comitatus allows the military to police cities; Insurrection Act forbids all domestic deployment
Posse Comitatus applies to state National Guard; Insurrection Act applies only to the Coast Guard
Both acts were invalidated in Marbury v. Madison
quiz.explanation: Posse Comitatus (1878) prevents federal armed forces from domestic civilian law enforcement, whereas the Insurrection Act (1807) grants the President authority to deploy troops to suppress domestic violence and rebellion.

quiz.q: What major event in 2001 triggered Georgia's historical realignment to Republican control with Sonny Perdue's 2002 election?
options: The adoption of open primaries by the Georgia legislature
Gov. Roy Barnes's legislative push to remove the 1956 Confederate emblem from the state flag
The establishment of Ranked Choice Voting in Atlanta
quiz.explanation: Democratic Gov. Roy Barnes's 2001 flag change sparked intense rural backlash, paving the way for Sonny Perdue (2002/2003) to become Georgia's first Republican governor since Reconstruction.

quiz.q: What does the Latin legal doctrine 'Stare Decisis' mean?
options: To stand by things decided (adhere to precedent)
The law is supreme over the king
To command an official to perform an act
quiz.explanation: 'Stare Decisis' translates literally to 'stand by things decided' and represents the foundational doctrine that judicial decisions should follow established legal precedents.
